clinicalPearls: Three mechanisms underlie osteomyelitis: hematogenous spread, contiguous spread after surgery or trauma, and secondary infection due to vascular insufficiency or neuropathy; in adults hematogenous disease most often involves the vertebral column, whereas in children long bones are seeded (Harrison 22e p.1061).

The clinically decisive distinction is not a fixed duration but the presence or absence of bone necrosis (sequestra): acute osteomyelitis without necrosis can generally be cured with antimicrobials alone, while chronic osteomyelitis with sequestra requires combined surgical debridement (Harrison 22e p.1062).

Back pain is the leading symptom of vertebral osteomyelitis (>85%), and the location maps to the level of infection (lumbar ~60%, thoracic ~30%, cervical ~10%); only about half of patients are febrile, partly because of analgesic use (Harrison 22e p.1062).

ESR and CRP are markedly more useful than the leukocyte count for screening: CRP is elevated in essentially all and ESR in ~98% of vertebral osteomyelitis cases, whereas leukocytosis and neutrophilia have sensitivities of only ~65% and ~40% (Harrison 22e p.1062).

In patients without sepsis syndrome, antibiotics should be withheld until a pathogen is documented (by blood culture, bone biopsy, or aspirated pus), because pretreatment markedly lowers culture yield and an established microbiologic diagnosis guides therapy (Harrison 22e p.1062-1063).

MRI is the diagnostic gold standard for vertebral osteomyelitis and should be obtained urgently when neurologic impairment is present to detect epidural abscess or exclude disk herniation; 18F-FDG PET is the alternative when MRI is contraindicated or implants/multifocal disease are suspected (Harrison 22e p.1062).

A primary focus is found in only about half of hematogenous cases; common sources are the urinary tract, skin/soft tissue, intravascular catheters, and the endocardium, and endocarditis is identified in roughly 10% overall (and in ~50% of viridans streptococcal cases) (Harrison 22e p.1061-1062).

Implanted foreign material creates a zone of local immunodeficiency and a host-protein-coated surface that promotes staphylococcal adherence and biofilm formation, so device-related bone and joint infection generally cannot be cured by antimicrobials alone (Harrison 22e p.1062, 1066).

Brodie's abscess is a subacute form occurring mainly in young males, presenting with pain (~98%) and swelling (~53%) in the tibia or femur, with a median diagnostic delay of about 3 months; localized unexplained tibial/femoral pain in a young patient warrants imaging (Harrison 22e p.1064).

Subacute or chronic vertebral disease is typically caused by Mycobacterium tuberculosis or Brucella in endemic regions, and by low-virulence organisms (coagulase-negative staphylococci, Cutibacterium acnes) in implant-associated infection; tuberculous spondylitis preferentially involves the thoracic spine (about two-thirds of cases) (Harrison 22e p.1062).

Synovial fluid analysis is central to diagnosing periprosthetic joint infection: leukocyte thresholds of ~1700/uL (knee) and ~4200/uL (hip) are about 90% sensitive and specific, and alpha-defensin is highly specific but limited by cost and sensitivity, so it should confirm rather than screen (Harrison 22e p.1066).

Chronic osteomyelitis can reactivate decades later; recurrence after a symptom-free interval exceeding 70 years has been described, most often in elderly patients with S. aureus disease acquired in the preantibiotic era (Harrison 22e p.1063-1064).
harrison.pathophysiology: Osteomyelitis is infection of bone reached by microorganisms via one of three routes. In hematogenous disease, circulating organisms seed the metaphyses of long bones in children and the vertebral column in adults; because the adult intervertebral disk is avascular, organisms enter through the segmental arteries supplying the adjacent endplates and then spread into the disk, producing the characteristic involvement of two contiguous vertebrae and the intervening disk. Alternative routes include retrograde seeding through the prevertebral venous plexus and direct inoculation during spinal surgery, epidural procedures, or trauma. Contiguous-focus disease follows bone trauma or surgery, with wound infection after sternotomy, open-fracture repair, or prosthetic-joint placement. Vascular-insufficiency/neuropathic disease, most often in poorly controlled diabetes, arises from progressively deep foot infection driven by ischemia of skin, soft tissue, and bone combined with motor, sensory, and autonomic neuropathy. Foreign material is highly vulnerable: host proteins such as fibronectin coat the device, favoring staphylococcal adherence and biofilm formation that resists phagocytosis and antibiotics. Failure of timely or adequate therapy leads to bone necrosis (sequestra) and progression to chronic osteomyelitis with sinus tracts and soft-tissue destruction (Harrison 22e p.1061-1066).
additionalDifferentials: Erosive osteochondrosis (most common MRI-based alternative diagnosis to vertebral osteomyelitis)
infectionMimics: Spinal epidural abscess from another source
Tuberculous spondylitis (Pott's disease) versus pyogenic osteomyelitis
nonInfectiousMimics: Seronegative spondyloarthritis (ankylosing spondylitis, psoriatic, reactive, enteropathic arthritis), including Andersson erosive diskovertebral lesions
Osteoporotic fracture and bone metastases on imaging
additionalInvestigations: CRP and ESR as sensitive screening/monitoring markers (CRP elevated in ~100%, ESR in ~98% of vertebral cases)
Blood cultures before any antibiotics (positivity 30-78%, heavily reduced by pretreatment)
CT-guided or open bone biopsy when blood cultures are negative, with aerobic, anaerobic, and fungal culture plus histopathology
Mycobacterial and brucellar testing in subacute/chronic, granulomatous, or epidemiologically suggestive cases
Nonculture molecular methods (eubacterial/multiplex PCR, metagenomics) when cultures are negative despite suggestive histology, to detect unusual organisms (e.g., Tropheryma whipplei, Helicobacter)
MRI as gold standard; CT to guide biopsy and assess sequestra; plain radiography useful mainly in subacute/chronic disease
18F-FDG PET when MRI contraindicated or multifocal/implant disease suspected (sensitive but not specific; useful to exclude PJI)
SPECT/CT with labeled leukocytes or antigranulocyte antibodies for osteomyelitis of >1 year duration; three-phase bone scan limited within ~1 year of surgery due to ongoing bone remodeling
Synovial fluid leukocyte count and alpha-defensin, multiple intraoperative tissue cultures/histology, and sonication of explanted hardware for biofilm organisms in suspected PJI
redFlags: New or progressive neurologic deficit (radiculopathy, weakness, sensory loss, bowel/bladder dysfunction, paralysis) suggesting spinal epidural abscess, present in about one-third of vertebral cases
Cervical or thoracic spinal involvement and S. aureus etiology, identified risk factors for severe neurologic deficit
Persistent or rising CRP, persistent pain, or sepsis syndrome indicating undrained abscess or treatment failure
Persistent pain after CRP normalization, suggesting mechanical complication such as severe osteonecrosis or spinal instability requiring orthopedic evaluation
Sinus tract, wound-healing impairment, or implant loosening signaling deep device-related infection
harrison.prognosis: Prognosis depends on early diagnosis, presence of bone necrosis, and whether an implant is involved. Acute hematogenous vertebral and long-bone osteomyelitis without sequestra or hardware can usually be cured with antimicrobials alone; a randomized trial in pyogenic vertebral osteomyelitis reported ~91% cure at one year with no difference between 6- and 12-week regimens. Failure of adequate treatment, open fractures, and unaddressed implant infection drive progression to chronic osteomyelitis with sinus tracts and soft-tissue damage. In fracture-related infection, implant-retention success falls with chronicity (about 86-100% in early, 82-89% in delayed, and ~67% in late infection). In periprosthetic joint infection, implant retention offers >80% infection-free survival only when the infection is acute, the implant is stable, the pathogen is susceptible to a biofilm-active agent, and the soft tissues are intact; in patients with severe comorbidity, lifelong suppressive therapy may be the chosen goal rather than cure (Harrison 22e p.1063-1067).
pitfalls: Starting empiric antibiotics before obtaining cultures in a non-septic patient, which markedly lowers culture yield and obscures the microbiologic diagnosis (Harrison 22e p.1062-1063).
Relying on plain radiographs or the leukocyte count in acute disease, both of which have low sensitivity; normal radiographs do not exclude acute osteomyelitis (Harrison 22e p.1062).

Using follow-up MRI to judge treatment response in uncomplicated cases, since radiologic improvement correlates poorly with clinical healing; imaging follow-up is reserved for pyogenic complications (Harrison 22e p.1063).
Misinterpreting a three-phase bone scan or 18F-FDG PET within ~1 year of surgery, when ongoing bone remodeling produces nonspecific uptake (Harrison 22e p.1064, 1066).
Assuming antimicrobials alone will cure device-associated osteomyelitis or PJI; without appropriate surgery such therapy is generally only suppressive (Harrison 22e p.1061, 1067).

Dismissing coagulase-negative staphylococci or Cutibacterium acnes as contaminants, when in the setting of an implant or prolonged bacteremia they may be the true low-virulence pathogens (Harrison 22e p.1062).
Failing to consider tuberculous or brucellar disease in patients from or traveling to endemic regions, where subacute/chronic vertebral osteomyelitis predominates (Harrison 22e p.1063-1065).
harrison.severityClassification: No single accepted comprehensive scheme exists. Osteomyelitis is categorized by pathogenesis (hematogenous, contiguous, vascular insufficiency/neuropathic), by course (acute versus subacute/chronic, with the presence or absence of sequestra being the decisive feature), and by location (long bone, vertebral, periarticular). The Cierny-Mader staging system classifies long-bone disease by anatomic extent, host physiologic class (systemic and local compromise of immunity, metabolism, and vascularity), and radiographic findings, and is used mainly to guide surgical management. Implant-associated disease is further classified by timing relative to surgery (e.g., early/acute, delayed, late), and periprosthetic joint infection is grouped for therapeutic decisions as acute hematogenous, early postinterventional, or chronic (Harrison 22e p.1061, 1066).
